parts.name: Mk1 Capsule
parts.desc: One seat, basic life support. Cramped but light.
parts.role: The cabin: one seat, the controls, and the air the crew breathes.
parts.detail: The smallest cabin that keeps a person alive: a seat, a window, life support for the trip and the computer that flies the ship. Light and cheap, but nothing spare: every extra bottle of oxygen is a part you add outside.

parts.name: Mk2 Capsule
parts.desc: Roomier cabin, better instruments.
parts.role: The cabin: the crew, the controls and life support, with room to move.
parts.detail: A roomier cabin with better instruments and a little more power. Still the heaviest single piece of hardware on most ships, which is why it sits on top: the rest of the stack is built to carry it.

parts.name: Mk3 Capsule
parts.desc: Big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.role: A big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.detail: The flagship cabin: more room, more power, a spare oxygen supply built in, and the most reliable systems. The price is mass, and mass is paid in propellant.

parts.name: Pointed nose, small
parts.desc: A slim ogive for a small stack.
parts.role: A slim nose for a small ship.
parts.detail: A small ogive fairing. Less frontal area means less drag in the thick air of the first two minutes, where most of the aerodynamic loss happens.
cons: Small: looks odd on a wide body

parts.name: Pointed nose cone
parts.desc: Low drag through thick air.
parts.role: A sharp nose that cuts through thick air.
parts.detail: The fairing on top of the stack. A pointed nose has the least drag in the thick air of the first minutes of flight, which saves propellant and keeps the aerodynamic load low.

parts.name: Pointed nose, large
parts.desc: A big ogive for a wide stack.
parts.role: A big nose for a wide ship.
parts.detail: A large ogive fairing for the widest bodies. More frontal area than the medium one, but the shape still cuts the air cleanly.
pros: Clean shape for a wide body

parts.name: Blunt nose cone
parts.desc: Cheaper and tougher, more drag.
parts.role: A rounded nose: cheaper, tougher, more drag.
parts.detail: A blunt nose is easier to build and takes a hit better, but pushes more air out of the way. The drag costs a little propellant on the way up.

parts.name: Hammerhead fairing
parts.desc: Wider than the body: room for a bulky payload.
parts.role: A fairing wider than the rocket under it.
parts.detail: A hammerhead fairing is wider than the stage below, so a bulky payload fits inside. Its own skin shields what is under it from one debris strike. The price: more drag, and a wide nose pulls the centre of pressure forward, so put bigger fins low.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Pulls the centre of pressure forward
parts.real: Atlas V 5 m fairing, Delta II 3 m "hammerhead"

parts.name: Payload attach fitting
parts.desc: The cone that bolts the payload to the stage.
parts.role: The standard interface between the payload and the stage under it.
parts.detail: A truncated cone with a bolted ring at the top and a clamp band at the bottom. It carries the whole payload through launch loads, then lets it go cleanly with push-off springs. Every launcher has a standard one, so a payload built for one rocket fits another.
cons: Mass that does no work after separation

parts.name: Spin table & clamp band
parts.desc: Spins the stage above like a rifle bullet before it fires.
parts.role: A turntable that spins the kick motor and payload for stability, and the band that releases them.
parts.detail: Small solid motors have no steering. The spin table turns the motor and payload to about 50 rpm before they separate, so gyroscopic stiffness keeps them pointed during the burn, like a thrown football. A Marman clamp band holds everything until pyrotechnic bolts cut it. Dawn was spun this way before its Star 48 fired.
parts.real: Delta II spin table and 3712 clamp band

parts.name: Kick motor, small
parts.desc: A Star-48 class third-stage motor in the stack.
parts.role: A compact solid motor that adds a final push.
parts.detail: The third-stage motor of the Dawn launch: a titanium sphere of solid propellant with a short nozzle, 66 kN for 87 seconds. Spin-stabilised, it needs no guidance of its own. Here it adds its propellant and thrust to the stack.
pros: Two tonnes of propellant in a small package
cons: Isp 286 s: worse than any liquid engine
parts.real: Star 48B: 66 kN, 286 s, 2,011 kg propellant, 126 kg empty

parts.name: Kick motor, medium
parts.desc: A larger spherical solid motor for the stack.
parts.role: A bigger kick motor: 3.3 t of solid propellant.
parts.detail: The larger spherical motor. Solid motors have the best propellant mass fraction of anything in the hangar (the case is 6 % of the mass), but the exhaust is slow: Isp 290 s.
pros: Best mass fraction in the hangar

parts.name: Ablative heat shield
parts.desc: Chars away to carry the heat off. Heavy and dependable.
parts.role: An ablative shield that chars away to carry heat off.
parts.detail: The ablative heat shield burns slowly and deliberately during entry, carrying the heat away with the charred material. Heavy, dependable, and the only thing between the crew and plasma.

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, large
parts.desc: A wider shield: more drag in thin Martian air.
parts.role: A wide ablative shield: slows the ship harder in thin air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that a wider shield matters: more area means more drag and a gentler, cooler entry. This one fits a large stack.

parts.name: Ceramic tiles
parts.desc: Half the mass. Chips if anything hits it on the way up.
parts.role: Ceramic tiles: half the mass, chips if struck.
parts.detail: Ceramic tiles insulate instead of burning away, so they weigh half as much. They are brittle: a piece of ice or foam on ascent can crack them, and a cracked tile on entry is how Columbia was lost.

parts.name: Inflatable heat shield
parts.desc: A stack of inflatable rings under a woven ceramic cloth. Huge area, new technology.
parts.role: An inflatable aeroshell: the widest shield for the least mass.
parts.detail: Packed small for launch, inflated to a wide cone before entry: stacked rings of woven fabric under a blanket of silicon-carbide cloth. The biggest drag area of any shield, which is exactly what thin Martian air needs. It has flown once, from orbit, in 2022, so reliability is lower.

parts.name: Supersonic parachute
parts.desc: Opens at Mach 1.7 in the thin Martian air.
parts.role: A supersonic parachute for the thin Martian air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that the chute opens at Mach 1.7 and still cannot slow the ship enough by itself. It buys time and speed before the engines light for the last kilometres.

parts.name: Drogue chute
parts.desc: A small, strong chute that opens first and steadies the ship.
parts.role: A small chute that opens early, stops the tumbling and slows the ship a little.
parts.detail: A drogue is small and tough: it can open faster and higher than a main chute, stop the capsule tumbling, and pull the main chute out. Alone it slows the ship only a little; with a main chute it makes the whole descent gentler.

parts.name: Splash floats
parts.desc: Keeps the capsule upright after the splashdown home.
parts.role: Keeps the capsule upright after splashdown.
parts.detail: Inflatable floats for the return to Earth: they keep the capsule the right way up in the sea until the ship arrives.
pros: Keeps the capsule upright at sea
cons: Only matters on the way home

parts.name: Low-gain antenna
parts.desc: Slow but it works from anywhere.
parts.role: Slow but works from anywhere.
parts.detail: A low-gain antenna: no pointing needed, a trickle of data in any direction. Enough for voice, telemetry and small files. Without any antenna nothing you find can be sent home.

parts.name: Medium-gain horn
parts.desc: A horn: faster than the omni, forgiving of pointing errors.
parts.role: A horn antenna: a useful middle between the omni and the dish.
parts.detail: A horn concentrates the signal into a wide cone. It needs only rough pointing, so it keeps working while the ship manoeuvres, and it sends data many times faster than the low-gain stick.

parts.name: High-gain dish
parts.desc: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.role: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.detail: A high-gain dish sends data hundreds of times faster, but only when it points at Earth. The science of the mission goes home through this.

parts.name: Relay smallsat
parts.desc: A small satellite left in Mars orbit to relay data home.
parts.role: A relay satellite released into Mars orbit: a dish in the sky even when Earth is below the horizon.
parts.detail: Every Mars rover talks to Earth through orbiters overhead. This smallsat rides on the side of the ship, is released into orbit, and relays data from the surface with its own dish and solar panels, so the crew can send science home even when Earth has set.
pros: Fast uploads from the surface, any time of day

parts.name: RCS thruster pack
parts.desc: Small thrusters to turn the ship in space.
parts.role: Small thrusters that turn the ship in space.
parts.detail: A reaction control pack: a cluster of tiny thrusters that fire sideways to roll, pitch and yaw the ship where there is no air for fins to bite. Needed to point the ship for burns and entry.

parts.name: Star tracker
parts.desc: A camera that reads the stars to know which way the ship points.
parts.role: A camera that finds the ship's attitude from the star field.
parts.detail: Gyroscopes drift. A star tracker photographs the sky, matches the pattern against a catalogue of thousands of stars, and tells the computer exactly which way the ship points, to a few arcseconds. Without one the dish and the burns are pointed by dead reckoning. Reliability +0.5 %.
pros: Exact pointing for burns and the dish

parts.name: Reaction wheel
parts.desc: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.role: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.detail: A spinning wheel inside the ship: speed it up and the ship turns the other way, no propellant needed. Slow and gentle; good for pointing an antenna, not for a landing.

parts.name: Spare O₂ tank
parts.desc: One EVA refill. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of O₂ a day.
parts.role: One spare EVA oxygen refill.
parts.detail: A high-pressure bottle of oxygen for the suit. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day; one bottle is one refill at the ship between walks outside.

parts.name: Oxygen tank, double
parts.desc: Two refills in one tank.
parts.role: Two EVA refills in one tank.
parts.detail: One tank, twice the oxygen: two refills for the suit. A little lighter than two separate bottles, because one valve and one mounting serve both.

parts.name: CO₂ scrubber
parts.desc: Keeps the cabin air breathable for months.
parts.role: Removes the CO₂ the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Without a scrubber the cabin fills with carbon dioxide in days. This one keeps the air breathable for months, the way the scrubbers on Apollo 13 did once the crew improvised a fix.

parts.name: Radiation shelter
parts.desc: Water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.role: A water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.detail: Between the planets there is no magnetic field to hide behind. When the Sun throws a storm, the crew climbs into this shelter, whose walls are tanks of water, until it passes.

parts.name: Water recycler
parts.desc: Recovers about 98 % of the water, like the ISS.
parts.role: Recovers about 98 % of the water.
parts.detail: Turns yesterday's water back into today's. The ISS recovers about 98 %; without it a long trip would need tonnes of water.

parts.name: Radiator panel
parts.desc: Dumps cabin heat into space; vacuum is a thermos.
parts.role: Dumps cabin heat into space.
parts.detail: Vacuum is a thermos: nothing conducts heat away. A radiator panel sheds the heat from electronics and people by glowing it off into space.
